title: Feeding black holes may help build rings of new stars
freshness: Published in The Astrophysical Journal and announced by the Center for Astrophysics on 14 September 2026, within the 15-day freshness window.
excerpt: MUSE maps of nine nearby galaxies show the same layout around their feeding central black holes: rings or arcs of new stars, cones of black-hole radiation, and fast shocks in the gas. The pattern suggests these black holes sometimes help compress gas into stars, alongside the better-known habit of heating gas or driving it off.
whyItMatters: Black holes are usually cast as the reason star formation shuts down. A repeated pattern of young-star rings, radiation cones, and shocks in nine galaxies points to a mixed local effect. The same outflow that disturbs gas may also help some of it collapse. The maps show the layout. The compression is inferred.

exploreFurther.label: Center for Astrophysics: New study reveals common pattern of black hole activity shaping nearby galaxies

whatToExploreNext: How energy from a feeding black hole can either sweep gas away or squeeze some of it into new stars.
body:
## The same pattern in nine galaxies

Nine nearby galaxies, each with a supermassive black hole still pulling gas in, show the same layout. Rings or arcs of new stars. Cone-shaped regions of energized gas. Fast shocks where outflows ram into that gas. The Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian announced the work from Cambridge on 14 September 2026, the day the paper came out in The Astrophysical Journal. The DOI is 10.3847/1538-4357/ae9956. A German-language account at scinexx is linked as another report of the study, not as a second dataset.

An active galactic nucleus, or AGN, is the bright center of a galaxy powered by gas falling onto a supermassive black hole. In the usual picture, energy coming back out heats gas or blows it away, and star formation shuts down. The new study says that picture is missing a direction. Actively growing black holes may also contribute to star formation in the host galaxy.

Nine is a modest sample, and large enough that the geometry is hard to file as one galaxy's quirk. The maps come from MUSE on the Very Large Telescope, which records optical light across a galaxy in space and in spectrum at once. Peixin Zhu, a graduate student at the Center for Astrophysics, says that once the galaxies were sharp enough, the black holes were seen pulling material in and throwing material out. The two motions are linked.

## Three colors for three power sources

The team used a three-dimensional diagnostic to separate, patch by patch, three ways to energize the gas. Star formation. Radiation from the active black hole. Excitation by shocks. A shock, in this paper's sense, happens when a high-speed outflow from the central black hole collides with the interstellar medium, the gas between the stars.

NGC 1386 is the galaxy they show as the worked example. In the zoomed map, red marks star formation, blue marks black-hole radiation, and yellow marks shocks. Across the full sample, star-forming rings or arcs appear about 0.8 to 6 kiloparsecs from the galactic center. A kiloparsec is their distance unit, thousands of light-years, so these rings sit well outside the nucleus and still inside the galaxy. Ionized cones of black-hole radiation extend outward from the disks. Regions dominated by fast shocks often run perpendicular to those bicones, the two-sided cones of radiation.

Zhu treats that right angle as the regular habit, not a one-off. The shocks go perpendicular to the direction of the black hole's injected outflows, and the arrangement shows up across all nine galaxies. The team reads the shocks as broadly consistent with jets from the AGN hitting the interstellar medium. Winds from the black hole may contribute as well, especially in galaxies whose jets are weaker. "Consistent with" is the right weight. The maps show where the shocks sit. The jet, or the wind, is the reading of why they sit there.

Lisa Kewley, an astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics, director of the center, and Zhu's advisor, describes black holes that do more than swallow material at the center. They reshape the surroundings. She frames the result as a look at a feedback cycle in galaxy evolution. Feedback, here, means energy leaving the black hole's vicinity and changing the gas that will or will not form the next stars.

## What was mapped, and what is inferred

Mapped with MUSE: the rings and arcs, the radiation cones, the shock zones, and the repeated right angle between shocks and outflows. Inferred: the same activity that stirs gas can also help compress some of it into new stars. Compression is a physical step between disturbed gas and a young star. The observations show the endpoints lined up in space. They do not follow one parcel of gas being squeezed and then lighting up. The inference is reasonable. It remains an inference.

Young stars have other reasons to form in rings. A bar, or a resonance in the disk, can pile gas up with no help from the black hole. The paper's case is that radiation and shocks sit with the rings in all nine systems, which would be a large coincidence if the nucleus were irrelevant. Closing that loophole is the job of the diagnostic and the models.

The study also compares the maps with theoretical models built by Zhu, Kewley, and Ralph Sutherland of the Australian National University, covering black-hole activity, star formation, and shocks. Chandra X-ray observations independently supported the reading. The announcement does not add a new X-ray number, so that support stays an independent check rather than a second map.

## A mixed local effect, not a new origin for galaxies

Gas falling into a black hole can release enough light and motion to empty gas from large regions. The same outflow can also hit a cloud along a shell or a ring and shove that cloud toward collapse. Both can be true in different places in the same galaxy. The nine-galaxy pattern is evidence that the second outcome shows up often enough to be a repeated structure.

Nothing here says black holes are net producers of stars, or that they assembled these galaxies. A net budget would need masses and rates the announcement does not give. The local claim is narrower: some gas is driven off, and some sits in a star-forming ring. The cycle the authors describe runs accretion, outflow, shock, and a change in where stars form.

The CfA release is the public account. The Astrophysical Journal paper is the authority for the measurements and the model comparison. scinexx is an additional report. Where the energy goes, and which gas it hits, decides whether the next stars are fewer or get a push.
